macro_actions.summary: The chapter outlines high-level phases and strategies focused on (1) assessment of patient symptoms and impairments, (2) creation of an empirically-supported, goal-directed treatment plan, (3) regular justification and reporting of treatment progress for managed care approval, and (4) adaptation of the treatment plan and report in response to changes in symptoms, progress, or life events. Therapists are guided to (a) define problems by evaluating symptoms (not deep underlying issues), (b) set measurable, observable goals, (c) select and document evidence-based CBT interventions related directly to symptoms, and (d) maintain frequent check-ins/updates to demonstrate progress and need for continued care.

micro_actions.summary: Therapists are instructed to (1) use DSM criteria to list specific symptoms, (2) document measurable impairments and changes session-by-session, (3) systematically record patient mental status using standardized dimensions (appearance, mood, affect, orientation, judgment, insight, etc.), (4) select and report CBT interventions matched to specific goals, (5) note rationales for any change in medication or therapy, (6) accurately and concisely complete treatment forms and reports for insurance approval, (7) highlight patient resistance or new stressors as they arise, and (8) track observable patient behaviors related to goals (e.g., completing exposure tasks, reporting symptom levels).

conversation_states.summary:
Key variables to track continuously include:
- Severity and frequency of specific symptoms (aligned to DSM criteria)
- Degree of impairment in social, occupational, educational functioning
- Progress toward each stated treatment goal
- Mental status features (appearance, attitude, consciousness, orientation, memory, psychomotor activity, speech, mood, affect, perception, thought content, thought process, insight, judgment)
- Patient’s response to interventions and any resistance
- New or ongoing life stressors affecting symptoms
- Medication usage and response
- Overall session-by-session improvement or deterioration

knowledge_graph.summary:
Long-term memory dimensions to track across sessions include:
- Patient’s diagnoses and comorbidities
- Historical and current symptom profiles, including severity and changes
- Trajectory of functional impairments in various life domains
- Progress toward and achievement of treatment goals (including relapse prevention)
- Interventions and outcomes associated with each goal
- Medication history and rationales
- Significant life events/stressors impacting symptoms or treatment
- Patient’s engagement, resistance, and response patterns

cautions.summary:
Therapists are cautioned against:
- Providing inaccurate or exaggerated diagnoses (“upcoding”) for insurance approval (unethical/illegal)
- Underdiagnosing, which may restrict necessary care
- Including more patient detail than necessary, risking confidentiality in reports
- Taking an adversarial or unprofessional stance with managed care reviewers
- Releasing information that contravenes state or HIPAA regulations
- Failing to record or justify changes in treatment, medication, or patient progress

macro_actions.summary:
- High-level dialogue phases and interventions for CBT for depression include:
    • Assessment (including diagnostic evaluation, symptom inventory, evaluation of suicidality, baseline measures, and exploration of comorbidities).
    • Socialization to treatment (providing psychoeducation, discussing the CBT model, collaboratively developing goals, and introducing expectations).
    • Behavioral activation (activity scheduling, reward planning, graded task assignment).
    • Cognitive interventions (identifying, monitoring, and challenging automatic thoughts, maladaptive assumptions, and negative schemas).
    • Skills training (problem-solving, assertiveness, social skills, communication).
    • Inoculation against future episodes (relapse prevention strategies, mindfulness, and MBCT).
    • Maintenance and phase-out (gradual reduction of session frequency, booster sessions, self-monitoring).
    • Troubleshooting obstacles (addressing noncompliance, hopelessness, self-criticism, rumination, insomnia).
    • Recommendations regarding medication, biological interventions, or alternative therapies.
    • Crisis management (suicidal risk assessment, no-suicide contracts, hospitalization decisions).

micro_actions.summary:
- Therapist micro-interventions at the utterance/interaction level include:
    • Asking direct, specific questions about symptoms, triggers, thoughts, feelings, and behaviors (e.g., “What happened before you felt depressed?” “What thoughts did you have when this happened?”).
    • Educating and guiding identification and categorization of distorted automatic thoughts (labeling, fortunetelling, catastrophizing, personalizing, etc.).
    • Using Socratic questioning to challenge thoughts (“What is the evidence for/against this thought?” “Would you apply the same standard to a friend?”).
    • Instructing in behavior tracking (completing activity or thought records, rating pleasure/mastery).
    • Assigning and reviewing homework (activity schedules, graded tasks, records of automatic thoughts).
    • Directly evaluating costs and benefits, semantic definitions, and alternative viewpoints of maladaptive thoughts and assumptions.
    • Modeling skills in-session, engaging in role-plays (e.g., reparenting, empty-chair technique).
    • Providing specific feedback and reinforcement for completed tasks/assignments.
    • Negotiating and clarifying homework difficulties and troubleshooting noncompliance.
    • Facilitating collaborative problem-solving during sessions.
    • Prompting self-monitoring of mood, energy, motivation, and sleep.
    • Making explicit safety/coping plans in cases of suicidality.
    • Reviewing and updating goals to maintain engagement and measure progress.

conversation_states.summary:
- Variables and features therapists should continuously track during sessions include:
    • Current symptom severity (depression, anxiety, suicidality, anhedonia, sleep, energy, etc.).
    • Suicidal ideation, intent, plans, behaviors.
    • Current and past moods and affect states.
    • Cognitive variables: automatic thoughts, underlying assumptions, core schemas, thought categories.
    • Behavioral variables: activity levels, avoidance/passivity, reward-seeking, self-reward/punishment, skills usage.
    • Social variables: relationship conflicts, social withdrawal, frequency of interpersonal contacts, social support.
    • Motivation, self-esteem, frustration tolerance.
    • Problem-solving and coping strategies currently in use.
    • Homework engagement/compliance, barriers to action.
    • Hopelessness, helplessness, indecisiveness.
    • Rumination levels (frequency, impact).
    • Comorbid symptoms/conditions (anxiety, physical illness, substance use).
    • Life stressors, recent losses, changes, trauma.
    • Sleep patterns and quality.
    • Medication adherence, side effects, changes.
    • Progress toward short-term and long-term goals.
    • Risk factors or warning signs for crisis/hospitalization.

knowledge_graph.summary:
- Long-term memory dimensions to track across sessions about the patient:
    • Diagnostic history (MDD/bipolar/other).
    • Number, duration, precipitating events, and outcome of previous depressive episodes.
    • Family psychiatric history (depression, suicide, substance use, etc.).
    • Core beliefs/schemas and how they originated (especially early life events, losses, patterns of negative socialization).
    • Patterns of maladaptive assumptions and automatic thoughts recurring over time.
    • Coping strategies, avoidance, compensation, behavioral and social skills deficits.
    • Relationship history (conflicts, social support, marital/couple issues).
    • Major life stresses/events and their impact (work, financial, medical).
    • History of suicidality/self-harm and previous safety plans/no-suicide contracts.
    • Medication trials, responses, and side effects.
    • Overall progress toward goals, relapse patterns, triggers for recurrence.
    • Motivational and behavioral patterns (habits, routines, reinforcement sources).
    • Personality traits relevant to therapy (e.g., obsessiveness, perfectionism).
    • Cultural/family/religious factors affecting beliefs and behaviors.
    • Goal history and achievement.

cautions.summary:
- Warnings or risks for therapists include:
    • Do not neglect or minimize assessment of suicidal ideation; always ask directly and set safety plans.
    • Do not use self-report forms or inventories as a substitute for thorough clinical interviewing.
    • Do not focus exclusively on one theoretical model to the exclusion of others; be flexible and patient-centered.
    • Do not assume patient insight into bipolar/hypomanic history; seek corroboration if needed.
    • Do not assign overly ambitious or overwhelming homework; tailor to patient's motivation and tolerance.
    • Do not reinforce negative interpersonal cycles (e.g., excessive reassurance in response to complaining—may worsen social withdrawal).
    • Avoid passivity or lack of structure in sessions.
    • Do not rationalize patient's self-criticism or hopelessness—challenge these patterns.
    • Do not ignore physical health, substance abuse, or comorbid conditions.
    • Do not allow abrupt cessation of therapy—phase out gradually.
    • Only qualified medical professionals should advise on medication, dosage, and combinations; therapists should not make medical recommendations beyond their scope.
    • Avoid reinforcing maladaptive perfectionism or avoidance (“must”/“should” statements).
    • Do not disregard patient's reluctance or resistance—explore it collaboratively.

macro_actions.summary: The high-level phases, strategies, and interventions performed by the CBT therapist for panic disorder and agoraphobia include: thorough assessment and diagnosis (including ruling out medical and comorbid conditions); psychoeducation and socialization to treatment; collaborative goal-setting; cognitive restructuring targeting automatic thoughts, maladaptive assumptions, and dysfunctional schemas; teaching coping skills (breathing retraining, relaxation training if needed); development and graded exposure to a fear hierarchy; elimination of safety behaviors; stress management and problem-solving; ongoing self-monitoring and homework assignments; phasing out therapy with relapse prevention; and troubleshooting common problems such as noncompliance and anxiety intolerance.

micro_actions.summary: Micro-level actions operationalizing these strategies include: conducting structured interviews and administering validated questionnaires; eliciting, identifying, and recording patients' automatic thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations in and between sessions (using forms and thought records); using Socratic questioning to challenge cognitive distortions and catastrophic misinterpretations; collaboratively examining evidence for and against thoughts and assumptions; designing and guiding behavioral experiments to test fears and safety behaviors; monitoring use and gradual withdrawal of safety behaviors during exposure; teaching and coaching patients in breathing and relaxation techniques (with caution regarding their use); guiding patients to create and practice exposure exercises (both imaginal and in vivo); reviewing and adjusting homework assignments; providing feedback and encouragement; tracking progress and modifying interventions as needed; and helping patients develop personalized coping statements and strategies.

conversation_states.summary: Variables and dimensions the therapist should track continuously during sessions include: number, severity, and frequency of panic attacks; situations/contexts and internal/external triggers for anxiety/panic and avoidance; subjective distress ratings (SUDs); use and type of safety behaviors; records of patient's automatic thoughts, assumptions, and schemas; patient's beliefs/confidence in the accuracy of thoughts; ability to cope/tolerate anxiety; homework compliance and progress in exposure tasks; physical symptoms and comorbid condition status; level of ambivalence about therapy; degree of anxiety intolerance; stressors and life events; and indicators of relapse or residual symptoms.

knowledge_graph.summary: Long-term memory dimensions to track across sessions include: patient’s diagnostic profile (including comorbid disorders and relevant medical conditions); history and course of panic, agoraphobia, and avoidance behaviors; personal and family history of anxiety, temperament, and relevant early experiences; cataloged feared/avoided situations and safety behaviors (plus their hierarchy); common cognitive distortions, assumptions, and schemas; progress and outcomes of exposure tasks and behavioral experiments; coping skills acquired and used; medication history and current regimen; frequency/severity changes over time (symptom trajectories); patterns of noncompliance or resistance; personal resources and inter/intrapersonal functioning; and any stressors or significant life events that relate to onset/maintenance.

cautions.summary: Therapist should not: neglect medical evaluation before starting treatment; use breathing/relaxation training as safety behaviors or for terminating panic attacks once begun; allow or reinforce reliance on safety behaviors during exposure or throughout therapy; prematurely terminate treatment before skills are acquired and maintained; overlook the importance of challenging cognitive distortions and assumptions; ignore potential comorbid conditions; pathologize or label the patient negatively; allow unrealistic expectations for rapid or complete elimination of anxiety; move therapy too rapidly for patient's readiness; skip homework review or proper rehearsal; ignore cultural factors and patient’s subjective experience; or assume cognition will change automatically through exposure alone.

summary.if: panic symptoms present and patient has not had recent medical evaluation
summary.then: refer for comprehensive medical evaluation before starting psychological treatment

summary.if: patient is beginning exposure to feared situation
summary.then: instruct patient to discontinue use of safety behaviors for that exposure task

summary.if: patient uses breathing retraining or relaxation as a safety behavior during panic or exposure
summary.then: redirect patient to tolerate anxiety and emphasize avoidance of safety behaviors

summary.if: patient expresses catastrophic misinterpretations about physical symptoms
summary.then: use Socratic questioning and behavioral experiments to collaboratively challenge and test these interpretations

summary.if: patient is unable to enter any feared situation without safety behaviors
summary.then: gradually incorporate and then phase out safety behaviors in the exposure hierarchy
reduce degree and complexity of assigned homework, review reasons and offer additional supports
schedule dedicated time in every subsequent session for homework review and progress feedback

summary.if: patient makes unrealistic expectations about full elimination of anxiety
summary.then: normalize anxiety and clarify therapy’s focus is on coping and tolerating, not total elimination

summary.if: patient presents with panic disorder and comorbid depression
summary.then: prioritize treatment of panic disorder unless depression is severe

summary.if: therapist learns patient uses medication or substances
summary.then: monitor use, assess for substance abuse or contraindications with therapy
track subjective units of distress and urge to escape; terminate session when misappraisals are disconfirmed or patient demonstrates tolerance

summary.if: patient shows anxiety intolerance or emotional perfectionism
summary.then: challenge through cognitive strategies, cost-benefit analysis, and psychoeducation on the normalcy of anxiety

macro_actions.summary: The chapter describes a comprehensive, multicomponent CBT intervention model for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), organized into progressive phases spanning assessment, psychoeducation/socialization, cognitive and behavioral interventions, interpersonal work, problem-solving, and phasing out/relapse prevention. Therapists are recommended to employ strategies targeting physiological arousal (via relaxation/mindfulness/biofeedback), maladaptive cognitions (worry, negative automatic thoughts, assumptions, and schemas), avoidance behaviors (exposure), intolerance of uncertainty, interpersonal deficits and emotional avoidance, and skill-building in problem-solving and assertiveness. Treatment addresses comorbidities as needed, tracks progress, and gradually moves to independent patient self-management.

micro_actions.summary:
- At each interaction, the therapist is expected to: 
  * Conduct detailed assessment and monitoring with standardized questionnaires (BAI, BDI-II, PSWQ, MCQ-30, IUS) and self-report logs
  * Provide psychoeducation on GAD and CBT
  * Assign and review homework (worry logs, self-help forms, bibliotherapy)
  * Teach and rehearse relaxation/mindfulness exercises in-session
  * Model and scaffold skill usage (assertiveness, behavioral rehearsal, role plays)
  * Guide cognitive restructuring: challenge automatic thoughts, test predictions, distinguish productive vs. unproductive worries, reframe catastrophic thinking, probe and modify maladaptive assumptions/core beliefs, and use cost–benefit, Socratic questioning, double-standard, and behavioral experiment techniques
  * Assign and structure "worry time" and stimulus control of worry
  * Formulate and review exposure hierarchies and reward plans
  * Use daily emotional monitoring and self-validation prompts
  * Direct patients in identifying links between thoughts, emotions, behaviors, bodily states, and relational context
  * Provide ongoing feedback, encourage positive tracking, and troubleshoot barriers (e.g., perfectionism, intolerance of uncertainty, resistance to exposure, demand for certainty/immediate results)
  * Facilitate skill generalization and relapse prevention planning

conversation_states.summary:
- The therapist should continuously track: 
  * Self-reported and observed severity/frequency/duration of worry and anxiety
  * Nature, content, and triggers of specific worry themes
  * Confidence in worry predictions vs. actual outcomes
  * Patient’s beliefs about worry (costs, benefits, function, danger, controllability)
  * Levels of physiological arousal and relaxation
  * Avoidance patterns and approach behaviors
  * Tolerance for uncertainty and intolerance-related distress
  * Emotional states and emotional schema attitudes
  * Interpersonal dynamics and problem-solving efficacy
  * Patient’s engagement, compliance, and motivation
  * Progress toward treatment goals and homework completion
  * Use/abuse of substances, sleep issues, comorbid symptoms

knowledge_graph.summary:
- Across sessions, the therapist should track and update information about:
  * Patient's baseline and ongoing scores on standardized measures (BAI, BDI-II, PSWQ, MCQ-30, IUS, others)
  * Core beliefs/personal schemas (e.g., about defectiveness, abandonment, responsibility, autonomy, approval)
  * Maladaptive assumptions/rules (e.g., perfectionism, certainty, control, approval, emotional intolerance)
  * Worry content themes and frequency patterns
  * Avoidance and exposure history, situational triggers and outcomes
  * Emotional schema features and emotional validation progress
  * Interpersonal skill development and relationship patterns
  * Problem-solving capacity, behavioral experiment results
  * Medication/substance use history and current status
  * Homework compliance, learning trajectory, and relapse prevention skills
  * Comorbid diagnoses and relevant treatment adaptations

cautions.summary:
- Therapists should avoid:
  * Premature termination of treatment, especially given chronicity and resistance in GAD
  * Reinforcing the belief that anxiety must be eliminated completely or immediately
  * Over-reliance on relaxation during exposure, which may reinforce avoidance of anxious states
  * Attempting to control or suppress all worried thoughts (may paradoxically increase distress and rumination)
  * Failing to differentiate between productive and unproductive worry
  * Ignoring comorbidities or substance abuse
  * Colluding with patient demands for certainty, perfection, or quick fixes
  * Using non-directive, purely supportive therapy without CBT interventions
  * Neglecting to monitor and address interpersonal, emotional, or schema-level issues contributing to worry

macro_actions.summary: Therapists follow a structured multi-phase approach for treating Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), typically including: comprehensive assessment (diagnosis, symptom identification, functional impairment, comorbidities); socialization to treatment (patient education, collaborative goal setting); cognitive restructuring (challenging dysfunctional beliefs, focusing on information processing errors); exposure interventions (imaginal, role-play, in vivo, with a focus on feared social cues, anxiety management, and dropping safety behaviors); optional social skills training and applied relaxation for those with skills deficits or strong physical anxiety; and phasing out treatment (gradual decrease in session frequency, relapse prevention, patient autonomy). The process is highly collaborative and adapts to specific patient needs (severity, comorbidities, progress).

micro_actions.summary: Therapists operationalize each phase with discrete conversational and behavioral steps such as:  - Asking open-ended, empathic questions to build rapport and gather detailed history  - Administering and reviewing standardized assessments and intake forms  - Providing psychoeducation, normalizing anxiety, and correcting misconceptions about SAD  - Directly eliciting automatic thoughts before, during, and after social events  - Guiding patients through structured thought records and Socratic questioning to identify cognitive distortions  - Modeling and coaching rational responses to distorted thoughts  - Collaboratively developing exposure hierarchies and selecting appropriate tasks  - Facilitating and debriefing imaginal, role-play, and in vivo exposures (including incorporating catastrophic elements, focusing attention on anxiety cues, and resisting safety behaviors)  - Conducting behavioral experiments (e.g., predicted vs. observed outcomes, deliberate demonstration of feared symptoms)  - Providing external performance feedback via therapist/group/comments, and video/audio review  - Shifting patient attentional focus from internal distress cues to external/environmental or goals-based cues  - Assigning, reviewing, and troubleshooting homework (thought records, exposure, social experiments)  - Identifying and intervening on safety behaviors and postevent rumination  - Using techniques such as vertical descent, survey of others, feared fantasy roleplay, and imagery rescripting for core schemas  - Gradually transferring responsibility and reviewing skills for real-world application and relapse prevention

conversation_states.summary: Therapists track a multidimensional set of variables throughout sessions, including:  - Symptom severity (anxiety and depression ratings via standardized scales)  - List and hierarchy of feared/avoided social situations  - Types and frequency of safety behaviors  - Content and frequency of automatic/dysfunctional thoughts (before, during, after events)  - Patterns of pre-event and post-event cognitive processing (anticipatory worry, rumination)  - Degree of distress and subjective anxiety (SUDs ratings) in specific situations  - Patient engagement and compliance (e.g., homework completion)  - Emotional/behavioral changes within and across sessions  - Comorbid disorders (e.g., depression, other anxiety, substance use)  - Functional impairment in social, academic, occupational roles  - Progress in skill acquisition (cognitive and social)  - Attentional focus (internal vs. external cues), use and dropping of safety behaviors

knowledge_graph.summary: Long-term memory dimensions to track across sessions include:  - Lifetime and current history of social anxiety symptoms (onset, triggers, developmental trajectory)  - History of comorbid psychiatric or substance use conditions  - Family history (genetics, parental/childhood influences, learned modeling)  - Significant adverse childhood/social events (embarrassment, humiliation, trauma, bullying)  - Patient’s individualized cognitive schemas and maladaptive assumptions  - Patterns of avoidance and safety behavior history  - Functional history in relationships, educational, and occupational domains  - Progress and remaining gaps in exposure hierarchies and skill acquisition  - Key memories or emotional events targeted by rescripting/analysis

cautions.summary: Therapists should avoid:  - Rushing assessment or pressing for full personal disclosure in initial sessions, which can heighten patient anxiety  - Interpreting avoidance or anxiety as non-compliance without considering the distress level  - Using relaxation as a replacement for exposure, especially as a safety behavior in patients fearful of physiological symptoms  - Failing to address or notice ongoing use of safety behaviors during exposure, which can maintain anxiety  - Over-pathologizing normal shyness or underdiagnosing SAD when presenting complaints focus on depression, substance use, or discrete fears  - Neglecting the role of comorbidities or core schemas (e.g., perfectionism, need for approval)  - Combining medication and CBT without clear rationale or without accounting for attribution of progress  - Tapering sessions before core therapeutic work and exposure hierarchy completion  - Failing to normalize the patient’s experience or to monitor for hypersensitivity to therapist's judgment

macro_actions.summary:
- Establish diagnosis of PTSD through assessment, including history of trauma, symptom profiling, and screening for comorbid conditions and contraindications.
- Socialize patient to treatment by providing education about PTSD, the treatment rationale, and available therapy and medication options.
- Initiate and conduct skills training, including relaxation, emotional regulation, and, if needed, interpersonal skills training.
- Implement exposure-based intervention (imaginal, in vivo, and cue-based exposure to memories and triggers).
- Conduct cognitive restructuring to address distorted automatic thoughts, maladaptive assumptions, and dysfunctional schemas related to the trauma.
- Address coping with life problems that may interfere with treatment, including social support and substance abuse.
- Phase out therapy by focusing on relapse prevention, reviewing progress, and planning for stressful events in the future.
- Troubleshoot common obstacles (e.g., resistance, overwhelming anxiety, noncompliance) and adapt intervention strategies accordingly.

micro_actions.summary:
- Elicit patient’s narrative of trauma in open-ended detail, prompting for specifics (sights, sounds, emotions, omitted details).
- Systematically assess and track PTSD symptoms using forms (PCL-C, trigger records, SUDs ratings).
- Guide patient through relaxation and breathing exercises, cueing to inhale/exhale and self-instruct "relax".
- Assign and review homework tasks (tracking triggers, exposing to "hot spots", listening to recordings, challenging automatic thoughts).
- Periodically prompt the patient for SUDs ratings during exposure and homework.
- Identify, log, and challenge safety behaviors, encouraging exposure without their use.
- Provide Socratic questioning to examine, challenge, or reframe cognitive distortions.
- Encourage monitoring and recording of progress, triggers, exposure outcomes, and cognitive changes across sessions.
- Engage in roleplays for interpersonal skills as needed.
- Modify exposure intensity and format (e.g., segment trauma, begin with less distressing cues, use written/external formats) based on patient readiness and response.
- Collaborate with patient in constructing exposure hierarchies and setting graded tasks.
- Reinforce and praise therapeutic effort and progress after exposure and cognitive shifts.

conversation_states.summary:
- Symptom severity levels (intrusive memories, avoidance, hyperarousal, distress ratings, comorbid anxiety, depression, substance use).
- Patient’s current emotional state and arousal level (SUDs, mood, anxiety, dissociation).
- Patient’s cognitive content: automatic thoughts, assumptions, schemas, negative beliefs, active cognitive distortions.
- Engagement in safety behaviors, avoidance patterns, and coping strategies.
- Patient’s readiness for exposure and skills training, and compliance with homework.
- Triggers (internal/external cues for trauma memories), including their distress levels and whether avoided.
- Social supports and psychosocial factors (relationships, substance use, crisis/stability, life problems).
- Phase within therapeutic plan (assessment, skills training, exposure, restructuring, phasing out).
- Intervention outcomes (reduction/remission of symptoms, cognitive modification, functional improvements).

knowledge_graph.summary:
- Patient’s trauma history (nature, timing, precipitating events, prior traumas).
- Patterns of symptom onset, chronicity, acuity, and progression (acute vs. chronic, delayed onset).
- Comorbid psychiatric history and prior treatment responses.
- Historical data on avoidance behaviors, safety behaviors, exposure outcomes, and symptom remission/relapse.
- List of triggers, "hot spots", cognitive distortions, and their evolution across sessions.
- Evidence of strengths and weaknesses (premorbid functioning), coping resources, and social support structures.
- Medication history and reactivity.
- Homework and intervention adherence logs.
- Patient's goals and tracked progress toward them.
- Relapse prevention skills acquired.

cautions.summary:
- Do not terminate exposure while patient is highly distressed, as it may strengthen anxiety associations.
- Avoid encouraging or allowing use of safety behaviors or coping skills during exposure tasks, unless temporary grounding is needed for dissociation.
- Do not proceed with PTSD treatment when patient has active substance abuse/dependence, is suicidal, or has unstable life circumstances interfering with participation.
- Avoid ignoring or insufficiently assessing for comorbidities, malingering, or legal/financial secondary gain.
- Do not minimize, rush, or invalidate patient’s description of trauma, distress, or cognitive distortions.
- Do not neglect relapse prevention in phasing out treatment.
- Avoid group CBT for PTSD unless specifically indicated (e.g., imagery rescripting for nightmares); individual therapy is preferred.

macro_actions.summary:
The chapter outlines a standard CBT intervention process for specific phobia comprising the following high-level phases and strategies:
1. Initial assessment and diagnosis (including differential diagnosis and identification of comorbidities).
2. Socialization to treatment—educating the patient about the evolutionary, behavioral, and cognitive models of fear, normalizing and depathologizing phobic responses.
3. Motivation building—exploring costs/benefits, patient goals for change.
4. Behavioral interventions—construction of a graded fear hierarchy, planning and conducting exposure (in vivo, imaginal, or interoceptive, adapted to phobia type), monitoring progress.
5. Cognitive interventions—identifying, challenging and restructuring distorted automatic thoughts and catastrophic predictions.
6. Elimination of avoidance, escape, and safety behaviors.
7. Homework—self-monitoring symptoms, exposures, and cognitive work between sessions.
8. Phasing out therapist support—fostering self-efficacy and self-directed exposure.
9. Troubleshooting—collaborative problem-solving for barriers such as patient reluctance, demands for certainty, limited stimulus availability, or therapist anxiety about exposure.
10. Relapse prevention and termination—preparing patient for future triggers and consolidating skills.

micro_actions.summary:
Operational actions for the therapist at the utterance/interaction step level include:
- Asking specific questions to identify feared objects/situations, automatic thoughts, avoidance and safety behaviors, and triggers.
- Providing psychoeducation about evolutionary models, phobia mechanisms, and exposure rationale.
- Collaboratively constructing and grading fear hierarchies using SUDs ratings.
- Using Socratic questioning and guided discovery to challenge catastrophic predictions and misappraisals.
- Directly eliciting, reviewing, and restructuring irrational thoughts (using forms, coping statements, and role play).
- Giving explicit instructions for imaginal/in vivo exposure and monitoring anxiety levels throughout the session.
- Coaching and troubleshooting efforts to eliminate avoidance, escape, and safety behaviors, including direct inquiry and arranging behavioral experiments on relinquishing these behaviors.
- Praising and reinforcing patient effort during exposures.
- Reviewing homework assignments in detail, and clarifying action plans for self-directed exposure.
- Providing feedback and normalizing emotional responses (e.g., sense of unreality after exposure).
- Supporting use of coping statements/cards in and between sessions.
- Fading therapist assistance, scheduling "overpractice" of exposures.
- Problem-solving barriers to compliance and anxiety management.

conversation_states.summary:
The therapist should track the following session-to-session variables/dimensions:
- Current severity and nature of phobic symptoms (specific triggers, anxiety levels, behaviors).
- SUDs ratings/fear levels for different stimulus situations and their progression over time.
- The patient’s avoidance patterns, escape behaviors, and safety behaviors.
- Automatic/catastrophic thoughts and their believability/distortion level.
- Degree of impairment in social, occupational, academic, or daily functioning.
- Comorbid disorders or substance use status.
- Patient motivation/engagement (including costs/benefits analysis for change).
- Homework compliance and progress in exposure assignments.
- Patient attribution of change (e.g., to therapist support, coping statements, or exposure success).
- Reliance on companions or external safety cues.
- Treatment phase (assessment, socialization, exposure, generalization, phasing out).
- Level of self-efficacy and readiness for increased autonomy.

knowledge_graph.summary:
Dimensions to be tracked across sessions about the patient include:
- Inventory of specific phobias, detailed content (objects/situations), severity, and avoidance behaviors.
- Individualized graded fear hierarchy (and its modifications over time).
- Record of exposure experiences: situations confronted, anxiety ratings, outcomes, catastrophic predictions vs. outcomes.
- Identified and challenged automatic/distorted thoughts.
- Catalog of avoidance, escape, and safety behaviors (and their status—abandoned/active).
- Homework compliance and outcomes.
- Functional impairment history: impact on social, occupational, and everyday life.
- Comorbidity profile (psychiatric, substance use).
- Medication history and adjunctive medication trials (if any).
- Relapse prevention strategies used and patient’s self-management skills.
- Evidence of generalization of skills (independent exposures, decreased reliance on therapist/companions).
- Patient’s motivational factors and changes in willingness to engage with exposure.

cautions.summary:
- Do NOT surprise or pressure patients into exposure with stimuli beyond their current tolerance or without collaborative agreement; exposures should always be predictable and under the patient’s control.
- Avoid attributing therapy gains solely to safety behaviors or external supports—foster patient self-efficacy.
- Do not reinforce avoidance, escape, or safety behaviors by permitting or ignoring them during exposure or homework.
- Avoid using relaxation exercises as a primary or regular strategy, as they may provide safety cues and impede learning (use only if patients cannot tolerate exposure at all).
- Do not dismiss patient fears as signs of weakness or cowardice; avoid stigmatizing language.
- Therapist should not act hesitant, afraid, or overly cautious about inducing anxiety, as this may reinforce the patient’s sense of danger.
- Do not guarantee absolute safety/certainty—frame risks in terms of probabilities, not absolutes.
- Avoid terminating exposure sessions before the patient achieves habituation, reduced misappraisal, or tolerates anxiety; premature cessation may increase sensitization.

macro_actions.summary:
The chapter outlines a structured cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) approach for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) characterized by several high-level therapy phases and strategies:

1. Assessment and differential diagnosis of OCD, including ruling out comorbid conditions.
2. Socialization to treatment: Educating the patient about OCD and CBT, building motivation, and normalizing symptoms.
3. Cognitive interventions: Using cognitive restructuring and guided discovery to modify maladaptive beliefs, schemas, and automatic thoughts related to danger, responsibility, perfectionism, and self-blame.
4. Behavioral interventions:
   - Exposure: Gradually exposing patients to obsessive thoughts, images, and feared situations (hierarchy-based, using imaginal and in vivo methods).
   - Response prevention: Blocking compulsive and avoidant rituals, either abruptly or gradually.
   - Behavioral experiments: Testing catastrophic predictions and appraisals.
5. Relapse prevention and therapy tapering: Preparing for maintenance, troubleshooting, and managing potential relapse.
6. Ongoing monitoring and troubleshooting: Addressing dropout, noncompliance, and lapses in ritual prevention.

micro_actions.summary:
- Conduct structured clinical interviews and standardized scales (Y-BOCS, MOCI, OCQ) for symptom tracking.
- Extract and log specific obsessions, compulsions, avoidances, and triggers as they arise in-session.
- Use Socratic questioning to challenge automatic thoughts, maladaptive beliefs, responsibility, and danger appraisals.
- Normalize intrusive thoughts by providing psychoeducation and reframing.
- Instruct patients in daily self-monitoring of obsessions, rituals, and emotional responses.
- Assign homework tasks: journaling, reading, self-help bibliotherapy, logging automatic thoughts and rituals.
- Construct exposure hierarchies and facilitate anxiety ratings (SUDs) during exposure tasks.
- Conduct imaginal or in vivo exposure within session, coach on repetition of exposures outside session.
- Guide behavioral experiments (e.g., intentionally thinking feared thoughts and tracking outcomes).
- Coach on disruption of rituals (e.g., delaying, slowing, altering ritual performance).
- Use behavior modification strategies: rewards, response cost, involvement of supportive others.
- Nonjudgmentally explore lapses, analyze antecedent thoughts, and plan corrective action.
- Advise and negotiate exposure/response strategies to accommodate patient’s motivational and tolerance levels.

conversation_states.summary:
Key variables and dimensions to track during sessions and inform dialogue management include:

- Presence, frequency, and severity of obsessions and compulsions.
- Avoidance behaviors and situations (active, passive).
- Emotional distress levels (anxiety, guilt, shame, mood scores from standardized scales).
- Patient’s insight/recognition of obsessions as unrealistic or excessive.
- Motivation and readiness for treatment/action.
- Feared consequences and catastrophic beliefs.
- Specific triggers (internal, external, situational, interpersonal).
- Quality of life and functional impairment (social, occupational, family).
- Patient’s appraisal of danger and personal responsibility.
- Compliance and engagement with exposure and ritual prevention tasks.
- Occurrence and nature of lapses or noncompliance.
- Support system involvement (family/friends).
- Progress along exposure hierarchies.
- Occurrence and intensity of negative automatic thoughts and schemas.

knowledge_graph.summary:
Long-term dimensions to track across multiple sessions (therapeutic memory/graph) include:

- Patient’s obsessive themes, types, and variants.
- Compulsive ritual types and patterns (frequency, intensity, triggers, contexts).
- Avoidance repertoire; specific situations/objects/people avoided.
- Feared (catastrophic) consequences and underlying beliefs.
- Automatic thought logs, cognitive distortions, schema profiles.
- Comorbid conditions (depression, anxiety, personality disorders, substance use).
- Medication history and current pharmacological regimen.
- Family members’ involvement in rituals or as support structures.
- Course of functional impairment (social, educational, occupational).
- Motivation history, treatment dropouts, and engagement levels.
- Exposure hierarchy progress (items mastered, current targets).
- Record of lapses, relapse events, and coping strategies utilized.
- Coping and relapse prevention plan; skills mastered.

cautions.summary:
Therapist warnings and risks highlighted in the chapter include:

- Do not provide reassurance during exposure as it constitutes ritualizing and disrupts learning.
- Do not allow patients to perform rituals after exposure, or during homework, as it undermines response prevention.
- Avoid being judgmental or critical about lapses; respond nonjudgmentally and use lapses as learning opportunities.
- Do not employ coping cards or standardized phrase repetition for cognitive restructuring if ritualizing occurs; vary the restructuring process.
- Avoid premature dropout by preparing patients fully and warning of relapse risk; do not neglect confronting most feared hierarchy items.
- Be vigilant for covert avoidance or mental rituals during exposure/response prevention.
- Do not proceed with ERP if the patient has "overvalued ideas" without first reducing belief in the obsessive fears.
- Do not ignore or fail to address comorbid conditions that may interfere with treatment (e.g., severe depression, substance abuse).

[

  {"if": "patient has severe comorbid depression or substance abuse", "then": "address comorbid conditions before starting or continuing OCD treatment"},

macro_actions.summary: The therapist employs various behavioral techniques to address depression and anxiety disorders. High-level intervention phases include: (1) assessment of skills/deficits and triggers; (2) psychoeducation/teaching concepts; (3) collaborative hierarchy/list/plan building; (4) therapist modeling and demonstration of target behaviors/skills; (5) patient role play/practice within sessions with feedback; (6) assignment of real-life homework for skill generalization; (7) regular progress reviews and refinement; (8) encouragement and reward of patient efforts. Core strategies: assertiveness training, behavioral activation, communication/social skills training, distraction, exposure/habituation (in vivo and imaginal), graded task assignment, mindfulness training, modeling, problem solving, relaxation/breathing exercises, self-reward, and visualization.

micro_actions.summary: Micro-interventions at the utterance/interaction level include: asking targeted assessment questions (e.g., for situations lacking assertiveness), teaching behavioral distinctions (assertive vs. aggressive vs. nonassertive), collaboratively rating anxiety/distress (SUDs, pleasure/mastery), guiding patients through listing/problem hierarchies and stepwise plans, providing clear instructions for skills (e.g., "use 'I' statements"), offering verbal/narrative models of behaviors, prompting specific role play or guided visualization/relaxation, giving constructive, immediate feedback (positive reinforcement/self-praise), challenging avoidance, cognitive distortions or inhibitory beliefs as needed, ensuring explicit, concrete messaging, encouraging return to focus (e.g., mindfulness), prompting tracking/recording via diary forms for exposures/activities, and providing specific homework instructions/reminders.

conversation_states.summary: Relevant tracked dimensions during the session include: patient levels of anxiety/distress (e.g., SUDs ratings), pleasure and mastery associated with activities, degree of assertiveness/aggressiveness/nonassertiveness in specified situations, patient knowledge/understanding of behavioral concepts/skills, engagement in rewarding activities, frequency and success at skill/behavior practice (incl. homework compliance), presence and type of cognitive barriers, degree of habituation/reduction in anxiety over exposures, patient use of avoidance/safety behaviors, goal/task progress, self-reward/self-praise behaviors, patient motivation and self-efficacy, moment-to-moment emotional responses, and appropriateness of social/communication behaviors.

knowledge_graph.summary: Long-term patient data to track includes: exposure hierarchies and progress (items mastered, current challenge level), behavioral activation activity schedules and mastery/pleasure ratings, assertiveness/social/communication skill inventories and their usage/transference across situations, catalogues of rewarding activities and self-rewards, history of practice and efficacy for relaxation/mindfulness/visualization techniques, records of problem-solving attempts and their outcomes, patterns of avoidance/safety behavior, successful homework completions and failures, evolving inhibitory/cognitive beliefs, and overall progress towards treatment goals.

cautions.summary: Do not terminate exposures before anxiety has reduced by half; do not allow/discourage safety behaviors or subtle avoidance during exposure (e.g., distraction, substance use, avoidance behaviors); avoid teaching distraction as a long-term solution or for OCD (where it may reinforce rituals); do not over-focus on relaxation techniques during exposure tasks (interferes with learning anxiety tolerance); do not set vague or unrealistic behavioral targets; avoid providing unclear/unmodeled instructions; do not punish or excessively criticize patient failed attempts—focus on reinforcement; do not push overwhelming tasks without grading them for achievability; avoid immediate rejection of patient brainstormed problem-solving options; do not invalidate the patient’s subjective experience in communication skills training; anticipate and guide patients from common pitfalls (e.g., waiting for motivation before activity).

macro_actions.summary: The chapter presents an extensive overview of high-level phases in cognitive and cognitive-behavioral therapy, focusing on interventions across a range of disorders (depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, phobias, etc.). Macro-actions include socializing the patient to treatment; collaborative assessment and agenda-setting; educating about cognitive-behavioral principles and symptom models (with handouts); identifying and collaboratively formulating problems and goals; ongoing assessment of symptoms and functional impairment; psychoeducation; employing cognitive and behavioral interventions (such as activity scheduling, problem solving, exposure, relaxation, mindfulness, and cognitive restructuring); continuously monitoring and challenging automatic thoughts, assumptions, and schemas; conducting experiential/role-play interventions; developing coping/self-instruction strategies; phasing-out treatment and relapse prevention; and collaboratively developing case conceptualizations tailored to the individual patient. The approach emphasizes active therapist involvement (guided discovery, Socratic questioning), homework, and an integrative, individualized treatment plan.

micro_actions.summary: Micro-actions encompass: eliciting and labeling automatic thoughts at the moment they arise; categorizing cognitive distortions; explicitly rating emotions and belief certainty (often on 0–100% scales); using structured questioning to challenge specific thoughts (e.g., examining evidence for/against, cost–benefit analysis, probability estimation, scaling catastrophes, considering alternative explanations, surveying others); completing structured records (event–mood–thought logs, self-monitoring forms); guiding patients through graded behavioral exposures; providing psychoeducation and instructions for relaxation/mindfulness; scripting self-instructional coping statements; role-playing new behaviors and responses (including in imaginal, in vivo, and reversed roles); supporting skill generalization between sessions through assigned homework; collaboratively revising assumptions and schemas through techniques like vertical descent, imagery rescripting, letter writing, and 'bill of rights' development; and delivering in-session feedback and validation.

conversation_states.summary: Key variables to track throughout the session include: current symptom severity and fluctuation (across mood, anxiety, behavioral domains); intensity, content, and frequency of emotions; type, frequency, and certainty of automatic thoughts; presence and strength of cognitive distortions; underlying maladaptive assumptions and schemas; current behavioral repertoire (activation/avoidance patterns, compulsions, safety behaviors, ritual use, etc.); motivational and engagement indicators (homework compliance, resistance, willingness to engage in exposures); situational/contextual triggers; functional impairment in social, occupational, and daily realms; patient’s insight and meta-cognitive beliefs about their symptoms or thinking; medication status/adherence and side effect profile; social supports and external stressors; ongoing tracking of treatment goals, outcomes, patient preferences, and feedback to inform the next action step.

knowledge_graph.summary: Long-term patient knowledge dimensions to maintain across sessions: diagnostic history and comorbidities; longitudinal record of symptom severity and course; schema maps and personal 'rule books' (core beliefs, typical distortions, learned avoidance/compensation styles); developmental history (notable adverse experiences, formative relationships, origins of schemas/assumptions); history of prior psychiatric treatments and outcomes; typical triggers, maintaining factors for symptoms (internal/external); record of progress with exposures and behavioral experiments; summary of effective and ineffective coping strategies; medication trials and responses; functional impairments over time; social network/supports; identified relapse risks; individual’s progression through treatment plan/goals; case conceptualization (including updates from developmental, cognitive, behavioral, metacognitive, and emotional schema perspectives).

cautions.summary: Do not rely solely on techniques without developing an individualized, theoretically informed case conceptualization ('trial-and-error' or 'shotgun' approaches are advised against). Avoid being purely technique-oriented or dismissing the value of the patient’s personal history and schema origins. Do not rush or force the identification of schemas or assumptions—these are harder for patients to access than automatic thoughts. Avoid minimizing patient distress or overlooking the depth of schemas behind surface symptoms. Do not foster dependence on safety behaviors or reinforce avoidance. Do not attempt exposures or challenging interventions without adequate socialization and collaboration. Avoid being invalidating, judgmental, or neglecting ongoing feedback and progress monitoring.
